claim: Volatile small molecules, including the short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), acetate and propionate, are released by the gut microbiota from the catabolism of nondigestible starches.
source: Volatile small molecules, including the short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), acetate and propionate, released by the gut microbiota from the catabolism of nondigestible starches, can act in a hormone-like fashion via specific G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific experimental data in this manuscript.

claim: SCFAs can act in a hormone-like fashion via specific G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs).
source: Volatile small molecules, including the short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), acetate and propionate, released by the gut microbiota from the catabolism of nondigestible starches, can act in a hormone-like fashion via specific G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: The primary GPCR targets for SCFAs are FFA2 and FFA3.
source: The primary GPCR targets for these SCFAs are FFA2 and FFA3.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Activation of both FFA2/3 in the lumen of the gut stimulates spinal cord activity.
source: Activation of both FFA2/3 in the lumen of the gut stimulates spinal cord activity and activation of gut FFA3 directly regulates sensory afferent neuronal firing.
evidence: This is a primary finding demonstrated through experiments using MOMBA and C3 in various mouse models, as shown in Figure 5.

claim: Activation of gut FFA3 directly regulates sensory afferent neuronal firing.
source: Activation of both FFA2/3 in the lumen of the gut stimulates spinal cord activity and activation of gut FFA3 directly regulates sensory afferent neuronal firing.
evidence: This is demonstrated through afferent nerve recordings showing C3 and TUG-1907 (FFA3 agonist) increase nerve firing, as shown in Figure 3.

claim: FFA2 and FFA3 are both functionally expressed in dorsal root- and nodose ganglia.
source: Moreover, we demonstrate that FFA2 and FFA3 are both functionally expressed in dorsal root- and nodose ganglia where they signal through different G proteins and mechanisms to regulate cellular calcium levels.
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunohistochemistry (Figure 4A, B) and calcium imaging studies (Figure 4C-F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

claim: FFA2 and FFA3 signal through different G proteins in dorsal root- and nodose ganglia.
source: Moreover, we demonstrate that FFA2 and FFA3 are both functionally expressed in dorsal root- and nodose ganglia where they signal through different G proteins and mechanisms to regulate cellular calcium levels.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experiments using FR900359 (Gq/11 inhibitor) and pertussis toxin (Gi inhibitor) showing FFA2 signals via Gq/11 and FFA3 via Gi (Figure 4C, D).

claim: FFA2 and FFA3 use different mechanisms to regulate cellular calcium levels in dorsal root- and nodose ganglia.
source: Moreover, we demonstrate that FFA2 and FFA3 are both functionally expressed in dorsal root- and nodose ganglia where they signal through different G proteins and mechanisms to regulate cellular calcium levels.
evidence: This is demonstrated through calcium imaging experiments with G protein inhibitors (Figure 4C, D).

claim: FFA2 and FFA3, acting at distinct levels, provide an axis by which SCFAs originating from the gut microbiota can regulate central activity.
source: We conclude that FFA2 and FFA3, acting at distinct levels, provide an axis by which SCFAs originating from the gut microbiota can regulate central activity.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the integration of multiple experimental findings including gut transit, afferent nerve recordings, ganglia expression, and spinal cord activation.

claim: The gut–brain axis allows bidirectional communication between the enteric and central nervous systems.
source: The gut–brain axis allows bidirectional communication between the enteric and central nervous systems.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: The intestinal microbiota plays a role in gut-brain interactions.
source: Growing evidence highlights the role that the intestinal microbiota may play in such interactions (Bienenstock et al., 2015) and in the development of disease (Luca et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The microbiota produces a wide array of metabolites that can modulate host cells and their functions.
source: The microbiota produces a wide array of metabolites that can modulate host cells and their functions (Chen et al., 2019; Nicolas and Chang, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SCFAs, particularly acetate (C2) and propionate (C3), are generated in prodigious amounts by fermentation of fiber and other nondigestible carbohydrates in the lower gut.
source: Among these short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), particularly acetate (C2) and propionate (C3), are generated in prodigious amounts by fermentation of fiber and other nondigestible carbohydrates in the lower gut.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: SCFAs play central roles in homeostasis at the interface between metabolism and immunity.
source: SCFAs play central roles in homeostasis at the interface between metabolism and immunity (Alvarez-Curto and Milligan, 2016; Tan et al., 2014) and within the gut–brain axis (van de Wouw et al., 2018; Dalile et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SCFAs play central roles within the gut–brain axis.
source: SCFAs play central roles in homeostasis at the interface between metabolism and immunity (Alvarez-Curto and Milligan, 2016; Tan et al., 2014) and within the gut–brain axis (van de Wouw et al., 2018; Dalile et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A range of key effects of SCFAs are believed to be produced by activation of G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs).
source: Although a range of their key effects are believed to be produced by activation of G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), both locally in the lower gut and following uptake into the systemic circulation, which of these roles are generated directly by individual receptors and via which signaling pathways and circuits remains undefined.
evidence: This is stated as current understanding in the field.

claim: FFA1 is activated by saturated and unsaturated fatty acids of chain length C10 and above.
source: Whilst FFA1 is activated by saturated and unsaturated fatty acids of chain length C10 and above both FFA2 and FFA3 are activated instead by SCFAs (Stoddart et al., 2008b; Bolognini et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Both FFA2 and FFA3 are activated by SCFAs.
source: Whilst FFA1 is activated by saturated and unsaturated fatty acids of chain length C10 and above both FFA2 and FFA3 are activated instead by SCFAs (Stoddart et al., 2008b; Bolognini et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Defining the functions of FFA2 and FFA3 is challenging due to overlapping potency of SCFAs at these receptors.
source: Defining the functions of FFA2 and FFA3 is challenging due to each of overlapping potency of SCFAs at these receptors (Hudson et al., 2012b), a paucity of highly selective pharmacological tool compounds for FFA2 and FFA3 individually (Milligan et al., 2017b; Milligan et al., 2017a) and multiple non-GPCR-mediated effects of SCFAs (Stoddart et al., 2008b; Bolognini et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: There is a paucity of highly selective pharmacological tool compounds for FFA2 and FFA3 individually.
source: Defining the functions of FFA2 and FFA3 is challenging due to each of overlapping potency of SCFAs at these receptors (Hudson et al., 2012b), a paucity of highly selective pharmacological tool compounds for FFA2 and FFA3 individually (Milligan et al., 2017b; Milligan et al., 2017a) and multiple non-GPCR-mediated effects of SCFAs (Stoddart et al., 2008b; Bolognini et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SCFAs have multiple non-GPCR-mediated effects.
source: Defining the functions of FFA2 and FFA3 is challenging due to each of overlapping potency of SCFAs at these receptors (Hudson et al., 2012b), a paucity of highly selective pharmacological tool compounds for FFA2 and FFA3 individually (Milligan et al., 2017b; Milligan et al., 2017a) and multiple non-GPCR-mediated effects of SCFAs (Stoddart et al., 2008b; Bolognini et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A transgenic knockin mouse line was generated in which a Designer Receptor Exclusively Activated by Designer Drugs (DREADD) derived from human FFA2 was expressed in place of endogenous mouse FFA2.
source: Firstly, in addition to the use of selective FFA2 and FFA3 knockout mouse lines we have extended the use of a transgenic knockin mouse line in which we expressed a Designer Receptor Exclusively Activated by Designer Drugs (DREADD) derived from human (h) FFA2 (Hudson et al., 2012a) in place of endogenous mouse FFA2 (Bolognini et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: The hFFA2-DREADD variant does not respond to the SCFAs C2 or C3.
source: This variant form does not respond to the SCFAs C2 or C3 and, therefore, both in vivo and in cells and tissues derived from these mice responses to C2 or C3 cannot reflect activation of hFFA2-DREADD.
evidence: This is a key characteristic of the DREADD construct, previously established and cited.

claim: Expression of FFA3 is unaffected in hFFA2-DREADD mice.
source: Importantly, expression of FFA3 is unaffected in these animals (Bolognini et al., 2019) and, therefore, effects of the SCFAs may instead be mediated by FFA3.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: 4-hexadienoic acid (sorbic acid) acts as an agonist at hFFA2-DREADD but is without activity at various wild-type orthologs of FFA2 and of FFA3.
source: In previous studies, we identified that 4-hexadienoic acid (sorbic acid) acts as an agonist at hFFA2-DREADD but is without activity at various wild-type orthologs of FFA2 and of FFA3 (Hudson et al., 2012a; Bolognini et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: Effects of sorbic acid in the transgenic mice are potentially mediated by hFFA2-DREADD but not by FFA3.
source: As such, effects of sorbic acid in the transgenic mice are potentially mediated by hFFA2-DREADD but not by FFA3 (Bolognini et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference based on the selectivity of sorbic acid, supported by citation.

claim: Sorbic acid has modest potency at hFFA2-DREADD.
source: Although we are unaware of any noted off-target effects of sorbic acid it has modest potency at hFFA2-DREADD and although it has extremely low toxicity (Walker, 1990), it is widely used as a food preservative (Kaczmarek et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of sorbic acid.

claim: Sorbic acid has extremely low toxicity.
source: Although we are unaware of any noted off-target effects of sorbic acid it has modest potency at hFFA2-DREADD and although it has extremely low toxicity (Walker, 1990), it is widely used as a food preservative (Kaczmarek et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Sorbic acid is widely used as a food preservative.
source: Although we are unaware of any noted off-target effects of sorbic acid it has modest potency at hFFA2-DREADD and although it has extremely low toxicity (Walker, 1990), it is widely used as a food preservative (Kaczmarek et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: A series of 4-methoxy-benzoic acid derivatives act as highly selective activators of hFFA2-DREADD.
source: Here by screening libraries of small molecules with similarity to sorbic acid we identified a series of 4-methoxy-benzoic acid derivatives that also act as highly selective, and somewhat more potent activators of hFFA2-DREADD.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the screening experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: 4-methoxy-benzoic acid derivatives are somewhat more potent activators of hFFA2-DREADD than sorbic acid.
source: Here by screening libraries of small molecules with similarity to sorbic acid we identified a series of 4-methoxy-benzoic acid derivatives that also act as highly selective, and somewhat more potent activators of hFFA2-DREADD.
evidence: This is demonstrated through concentration-response curves in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: 4-methoxy-3-methyl-benzoic acid (MOMBA) was selected for the studies.
source: From these we selected 4-methoxy-3-methyl-benzoic acid (MOMBA) for the studies reported herein.
evidence: This is stated explicitly in the introduction.

claim: Combinations of FFA2 and FFA3 transduce different effects of SCFAs within gut-brain pathways.
source: We show that combinations of these two receptors transduce different effects of SCFAs within these pathways and via different G-protein-mediated pathways and, by so doing, integrate signals to control the microbiota–gut–brain axis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the integration of multiple experimental findings throughout the manuscript.

claim: FFA2 and FFA3 integrate signals to control the microbiota–gut–brain axis via different G-protein-mediated pathways.
source: We show that combinations of these two receptors transduce different effects of SCFAs within these pathways and via different G-protein-mediated pathways and, by so doing, integrate signals to control the microbiota–gut–brain axis.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experiments showing FFA2 signals via Gq/11 and FFA3 via Gi (Figure 4C, D).

claim: Sorbic acid promoted interactions between hFFA2-DREADD and β-arrestin-2 in a concentration-dependent manner with pEC50 = 3.89 ± 0.04.
source: Using sorbic acid as a positive control, BRET signal was enhanced in a concentration-dependent manner with pEC50 = 3.89 ± 0.04 (n = 3, mean ± standard deviation [SD], Figure 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through BRET assay data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The screening assay had a calculated Z′ routinely >0.6.
source: This provided a robust 96-well microtitre plate-based assay with calculated Z′ (Zhang et al., 1999) routinely >0.6 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) and greater than fivefold signal to background (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through assay validation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The screening assay had greater than fivefold signal to background.
source: This provided a robust 96-well microtitre plate-based assay with calculated Z′ (Zhang et al., 1999) routinely >0.6 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) and greater than fivefold signal to background (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through assay validation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Compound 565 (MOMBA) and compound 1184 (sorbic acid) were identified as positives in reconfirmation screens.
source: Reconfirmation screens of potential hits, also conducted at 100 µM, provided positives, including compounds 565 and 1184 (Figure 1B). Deconvolution indicated that compound 1184 was, in fact, sorbic acid, confirming the capacity of the screen to identify effectively a previously characterized active, whilst compound 565 was MOMBA (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through screening data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 4-methoxy-3-chloro-benzoic acid (compound 132) and 4-methoxy-3-hydroxy-benzoic acid (compound 235) were identified as actives in the second round of screening.
source: This resulted in the identification of further compounds including a number closely related to MOMBA, such as 4-methoxy-3-chloro-benzoic acid (compound 132) and 4-methoxy-3-hydroxy-benzoic acid (compound 235) as actives (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through screening data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Some of the identified compounds were at least as potent as sorbic acid with the best displaying some three- to fivefold higher potency.
source: A number of these were at least as potent as sorbic acid with the best displaying some three- to fivefold higher potency in this assay (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through concentration-response data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: MOMBA was without detectable activity at wild-type human FFA2 in a BRET-based receptor–β-arrestin-2 interaction assay.
source: Following transient coexpression of hFFA2-eYFP and β-arrestin-2-Renilla-luciferase in HEK293 cells, whilst the SCFA propionate (C3) was an effective agonist with pEC50 = 3.46 ± 0.01 (n = 3) MOMBA was without detectable activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through BRET assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: C3 inhibited forskolin-amplified cAMP levels in cells expressing human FFA2, but neither sorbic acid nor MOMBA did so.
source: In Flp-In T-REx 293 cells stably expressing hFFA2-eYFP, C3 inhibited forskolin-amplified cAMP levels, but neither sorbic acid nor MOMBA did so (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through cAMP inhibition assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: In cells expressing mouse FFA2, only C3 but not either sorbic acid or MOMBA was able to inhibit forskolin-amplified cAMP levels.
source: Equivalent results were produced in Flp-In T-REx 293 cells induced to express mouse FFA2-eYFP where again only C3 but not either sorbic acid or MOMBA was able to inhibit forskolin-amplified cAMP levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through cAMP inhibition assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: C3 inhibited cAMP levels in cells expressing either human or murine FFA3, whilst no effect of sorbic acid or MOMBA was observed.
source: Using Flp-In T-REx 293 cells expressing either human or murine forms of FFA3-eYFP C3 inhibited cAMP levels whilst, again, no effect of sorbic acid or MOMBA was observed (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through cAMP inhibition assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: MOMBA inhibited forskolin-stimulated cAMP levels in cells expressing hFFA2-DREADD with pEC50 = 5.24 ± 0.16.
source: The inhibition of forskolin-stimulated cAMP levels by MOMBA in cells expressing the hFFA2-DREADD receptor was concentration-dependent and MOMBA was more potent (pEC50 = 5.24 ± 0.16, mean ± SD, n = 3) than sorbic acid (pEC50 = 4.77 ± 0.15, mean ± SD, n = 3) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through cAMP inhibition assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Sorbic acid inhibited forskolin-stimulated cAMP levels in cells expressing hFFA2-DREADD with pEC50 = 4.77 ± 0.15.
source: The inhibition of forskolin-stimulated cAMP levels by MOMBA in cells expressing the hFFA2-DREADD receptor was concentration-dependent and MOMBA was more potent (pEC50 = 5.24 ± 0.16, mean ± SD, n = 3) than sorbic acid (pEC50 = 4.77 ± 0.15, mean ± SD, n = 3) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through cAMP inhibition assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: C3 was unable to promote inositol monophosphate generation in Flp-In T-REx 293 cells expressing hFFA2-DREADD.
source: We established, therefore, that although C3 was unable to promote inositol monophosphate generation in Flp-In T-REx 293 cells expressing hFFA2-DREADD (Bolognini et al., 2019), MOMBA again did so in a concentration-dependent manner and with both potency and efficacy at least equivalent to sorbic acid (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work and demonstrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: MOMBA promoted inositol monophosphate generation in cells expressing hFFA2-DREADD in a concentration-dependent manner with potency and efficacy at least equivalent to sorbic acid.
source: We established, therefore, that although C3 was unable to promote inositol monophosphate generation in Flp-In T-REx 293 cells expressing hFFA2-DREADD (Bolognini et al., 2019), MOMBA again did so in a concentration-dependent manner and with both potency and efficacy at least equivalent to sorbic acid (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through inositol monophosphate assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: MOMBA and sorbic acid stimulated binding of [35S]GTPγS in membranes from cells expressing hFFA2-DREADD.
source: These characteristics were reiterated in measures of ligand-regulated binding of [35S]GTPγS performed on membranes from Flp-In T-REx 293 cells expressing hFFA2-DREADD (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through [35S]GTPγS binding assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: The effect of MOMBA to stimulate [35S]GTPγS binding was fully inhibited by GLPG0974 with pIC50 = 7.58 ± 0.07.
source: The effect of an EC80 concentration of MOMBA to stimulate [35S]GTPγS binding was fully inhibited by increasing concentrations of both of the structurally distinct, human FFA2 ortholog specific, antagonists 4-[[[(2R)-1-(benzo[b]thien-3-ylcarbonyl)–2-methyl-2-azetidinyl]carbonyl][(3-chlorophenyl)methyl]amino]butanoic acid (GLPG0974) (pIC50 = 7.58 ± 0.07, mean ± standard error of the mean [SEM], n = 3) and ((S)-3-(2-(3-chlorophenyl)acetamido)-4-(4-(trifluoromethyl)phenyl)butanoic acid) (CATPB) (pIC50 = 7.63 ± 0.08, mean ± SEM, n = 3) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through antagonist inhibition data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D.

claim: The effect of MOMBA to stimulate [35S]GTPγS binding was fully inhibited by CATPB with pIC50 = 7.63 ± 0.08.
source: The effect of an EC80 concentration of MOMBA to stimulate [35S]GTPγS binding was fully inhibited by increasing concentrations of both of the structurally distinct, human FFA2 ortholog specific, antagonists 4-[[[(2R)-1-(benzo[b]thien-3-ylcarbonyl)–2-methyl-2-azetidinyl]carbonyl][(3-chlorophenyl)methyl]amino]butanoic acid (GLPG0974) (pIC50 = 7.58 ± 0.07, mean ± standard error of the mean [SEM], n = 3) and ((S)-3-(2-(3-chlorophenyl)acetamido)-4-(4-(trifluoromethyl)phenyl)butanoic acid) (CATPB) (pIC50 = 7.63 ± 0.08, mean ± SEM, n = 3) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through antagonist inhibition data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D.

claim: MOMBA likely binds in the orthosteric pocket of hFFA2-DREADD.
source: This is consistent with, as for sorbic acid (Bolognini et al., 2019), MOMBA likely binding in the orthosteric pocket of hFFA2-DREADD.
evidence: This is inferred from the antagonist inhibition data and comparison to sorbic acid.

claim: MOMBA and sorbic acid lacked activity at the Arg180Ala mutant of hFFA2-DREADD.
source: Whilst both MOMBA- and sorbic acid-stimulated hFFA2-DREADD activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E), MOMBA, as well as sorbic acid, lacked activity at the Arg180Ala mutant of hFFA2-DREADD (Figure 1—figure supplement 3F).
evidence: This is demonstrated through [35S]GTPγS binding assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3F.

claim: The allosteric agonist AZ1729 was equipotent at both wild type and the Arg180Ala mutant of hFFA2-DREADD.
source: By contrast, a previously described allosteric agonist AZ1729 (Bolognini et al., 2016a) that does not require Arg180 for binding and function was equipotent at both wild type and the Arg180Ala mutant of hFFA2-DREADD (Figure 1—figure supplement 3F).
evidence: This is demonstrated through [35S]GTPγS binding assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3F.

claim: 21.8 ± 8.1% of HuC/D-positive enteric neurons in myenteric plexus from FFA2-KO-βGAL mice showed β-galactosidase staining.
source: Fluorescent X-gal staining in myenteric plexus dissected from FFA2-KO-βGAL (21.8 ± 8.1%) (Figure 2A, upper panel) and FFA3-KO-βGAL mice (34.3 ± 5.6%) (Figure 2A, lower panel) (means ± SEM) revealed gene expression in enteric neurons as defined by staining for the neuronal RNA-binding proteins HuC/D (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 34.3 ± 5.6% of HuC/D-positive enteric neurons in myenteric plexus from FFA3-KO-βGAL mice showed β-galactosidase staining.
source: Fluorescent X-gal staining in myenteric plexus dissected from FFA2-KO-βGAL (21.8 ± 8.1%) (Figure 2A, upper panel) and FFA3-KO-βGAL mice (34.3 ± 5.6%) (Figure 2A, lower panel) (means ± SEM) revealed gene expression in enteric neurons as defined by staining for the neuronal RNA-binding proteins HuC/D (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: β-Galactosidase staining was not found in enteric glia as defined by staining for GFAP.
source: β-Galactosidase staining was not found in enteric glia as defined by staining for Glial Fibrillary Acidic Protein (GFAP) (Figure 2A, right-hand panels).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Oral administration of MOMBA (15 mM) in the drinking water of hFFA2-DREADD-HA-expressing mice significantly reduced gut transit.
source: Entirely consistent with our previous studies with sorbic acid (Bolognini et al., 2019) we established that oral administration of MOMBA (15 mM) in the drinking water of hFFA2-DREADD-HA-expressing mice significantly reduced (p < 0.01) gut transit (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through gut transit measurements shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Provision of MOMBA in the drinking water of CRE-Minus mice did not affect gut transit.
source: This clearly was an on-target hFFA2-DREADD-mediated effect because provision of MOMBA in the drinking water of CRE-Minus mice did not replicate this effect (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through gut transit measurements shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Provision of C3 propionate in the drinking water significantly reduced GI transit in FFA2-KO-βGAL mice.
source: Furthermore, as we also observed a significant reduction (p < 0.05) in GI transit after provision of the C3 SCFA propionate in the drinking water of both FFA2-KO-βGAL (Figure 2D) and FFA3-KO-βGAL (Figure 2E) mice, this suggests that both the FFA2 and FFA3 receptors play roles in controlling muscle function.
evidence: This is demonstrated through gut transit measurements shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Provision of C3 propionate in the drinking water significantly reduced GI transit in FFA3-KO-βGAL mice.
source: Furthermore, as we also observed a significant reduction (p < 0.05) in GI transit after provision of the C3 SCFA propionate in the drinking water of both FFA2-KO-βGAL (Figure 2D) and FFA3-KO-βGAL (Figure 2E) mice, this suggests that both the FFA2 and FFA3 receptors play roles in controlling muscle function.
evidence: This is demonstrated through gut transit measurements shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Both FFA2 and FFA3 receptors play roles in controlling muscle function.
source: Furthermore, as we also observed a significant reduction (p < 0.05) in GI transit after provision of the C3 SCFA propionate in the drinking water of both FFA2-KO-βGAL (Figure 2D) and FFA3-KO-βGAL (Figure 2E) mice, this suggests that both the FFA2 and FFA3 receptors play roles in controlling muscle function.
evidence: This is inferred from the gut transit data in knockout mice.

claim: MOMBA promoted a concentration-dependent release of GLP-1 from colonic crypts prepared from hFFA2-DREADD-HA mice.
source: Consistent with these studies, and to further define the suitability of MOMBA for subsequent ex vivo studies, we show here that MOMBA also promoted a concentration-dependent release of GLP-1 from colonic crypts prepared from hFFA2-DREADD-HA mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through GLP-1 release assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: At 100 µM MOMBA was as effective as 1 mM sorbic acid in promoting GLP-1 release from colonic crypts.
source: Moreover, at 100 µM MOMBA was as effective as 1 mM sorbic acid (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), consistent with the higher potency of MOMBA measured in vitro (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated through GLP-1 release assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: C3 (10 mM) was unable to induce release of GLP-1 from hFFA2-DREADD-HA colonic crypts.
source: These studies also indicated that MOMBA was at least as efficacious as sorbic acid in native cells and tissues. In control experiments C3 (10 mM) was unable to induce release of GLP-1 from hFFA2-DREADD-HA colonic crypts as expected (Bolognini et al., 2019), eliminating a role for FFA3.
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work.

claim: MOMBA caused a rapid and sustained increase in the release of GLP-1 from colonic tissue in an organ bath preparation.
source: In this preparation MOMBA caused a rapid and sustained increase in the release of GLP-1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) in a manner that was completely inhibited by the hFFA2-specific antagonist CATPB (Bolognini et al., 2019; Sergeev et al., 2016) a ligand that also antagonizes the hFFA2-DREADD (see Bolognini et al., 2019 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through organ bath GLP-1 release data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The effect of MOMBA on GLP-1 release was completely inhibited by CATPB.
source: In this preparation MOMBA caused a rapid and sustained increase in the release of GLP-1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) in a manner that was completely inhibited by the hFFA2-specific antagonist CATPB (Bolognini et al., 2019; Sergeev et al., 2016) a ligand that also antagonizes the hFFA2-DREADD (see Bolognini et al., 2019 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through organ bath GLP-1 release data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: MOMBA was unable to promote release of GLP-1 from colonic tissue obtained from CRE-MINUS animals.
source: In colonic tissue from such CRE-MINUS animals MOMBA was unable to promote release of GLP-1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), further confirming this endpoint to reflect activation of hFFA2-DREADD rather than any potential 'off-target', nonreceptor, mediated effect of MOMBA.
evidence: This is demonstrated through organ bath GLP-1 release data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Perfusion of colonic tubes isolated from hFFA2-DREADD-HA mice with MOMBA resulted in a rapid, markedly enhanced, but transient, release of PYY.
source: Peptide YY (PYY) is expressed in similar subsets of enteroendocrine 'L-cells' as GLP-1 (Nohr et al., 2013; Lu et al., 2018) and perfusion of colonic tubes isolated from hFFA2-DREADD-HA mice with MOMBA also resulted in a rapid, markedly enhanced (p < 0.01), but in this case transient, release of PYY (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through organ bath PYY release data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The effect of MOMBA on PYY release was not observed in the presence of CATPB.
source: This effect of MOMBA was not observed in the presence of CATPB (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D) and was also not produced in equivalent preparations generated from CRE-MINUS animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated through organ bath PYY release data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: MOMBA did not promote PYY release in preparations generated from CRE-MINUS animals.
source: This effect of MOMBA was not observed in the presence of CATPB (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D) and was also not produced in equivalent preparations generated from CRE-MINUS animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated through organ bath PYY release data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: A subset of PYY-expressing cells in colonic sections from hFFA2-DREADD-HA mice also expressed hFFA2-DREADD-HA.
source: Consistent with the MOMBA-induced release of PYY, costaining of colonic sections from the hFFA2-DREADD-HA mice with both anti-HA and anti-PYY antibodies identified a subset of cells that as well as being positive for PYY also expressed hFFA2-DREADD-HA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Perfusion of tissue from wild-type mice with C3 resulted in a marked increase in rate of nerve firing in proximal colon preparations.
source: Perfusion of tissue with C3 resulted in a marked increase (p < 0.01) in rate of nerve firing in this preparation (Figure 3B, C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through afferent nerve recording data shown in Figure 3B, C.

claim: C3 produced a similar increase in nerve firing in tissue isolated from hFFA2-DREADD-HA-expressing mice.
source: C3 produced a similar effect (p < 0.05) in tissue isolated from hFFA2-DREADD-HA-expressing mice (Figure 3C) potentially indicating a key role for FFA3.
evidence: This is demonstrated through afferent nerve recording data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: No statistically significant effect of MOMBA on nerve firing was observed in tissue from hFFA2-DREADD-HA-expressing mice.
source: However, no statistically significant effect of MOMBA was observed (Figure 3D) and this was also the case when MOMBA was applied to tissue taken from the CRE-MINUS animals (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through afferent nerve recording data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: MOMBA did not affect nerve firing in tissue from CRE-MINUS animals.
source: However, no statistically significant effect of MOMBA was observed (Figure 3D) and this was also the case when MOMBA was applied to tissue taken from the CRE-MINUS animals (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through afferent nerve recording data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: FFA2 does not contribute significantly to the observed effects of C3 on nerve firing in wild-type mice.
source: This combination of studies indicates that FFA2 does not contribute significantly to the observed effects of C3 in wild-type mice but would be consistent with a specific role for FFA3.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of effect of MOMBA on nerve firing.

claim: TUG-1907 increased nerve activity in tissue from C57/BL/6 mice.
source: TUG-1907 increased nerve activity in tissue from C57/BL/6 mice (p < 0.01), but this was absent in tissue from FFA3-KO-βGAL mice, confirming the role of FFA3 in increasing peripheral nerve activity from the proximal colon in response to SCFAs.
evidence: This is demonstrated through afferent nerve recording data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: TUG-1907 did not increase nerve activity in tissue from FFA3-KO-βGAL mice.
source: TUG-1907 increased nerve activity in tissue from C57/BL/6 mice (p < 0.01), but this was absent in tissue from FFA3-KO-βGAL mice, confirming the role of FFA3 in increasing peripheral nerve activity from the proximal colon in response to SCFAs.
evidence: This is demonstrated through afferent nerve recording data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: FFA3 plays a role in increasing peripheral nerve activity from the proximal colon in response to SCFAs.
source: TUG-1907 increased nerve activity in tissue from C57/BL/6 mice (p < 0.01), but this was absent in tissue from FFA3-KO-βGAL mice, confirming the role of FFA3 in increasing peripheral nerve activity from the proximal colon in response to SCFAs.
evidence: This is concluded from the TUG-1907 experiments in wild-type and FFA3-KO mice.

claim: Anti-HA staining of NDG isolated from hFFA2-DREADD-HA mice showed clear immunoreactivity that overlapped to only a limited degree with the neuronal marker PGP9.5 (7.5 ± 3.8%).
source: Anti-HA staining of NDG isolated from hFFA2-DREADD-HA mice showed clear immunoreactivity that overlapped to only a limited degree with the neuronal marker PGP9.5 (7.5 ± 3.8% [mean ± SEM]; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and was also noted in various cells located between the neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 37.2 ± 8.4% of cells from NDG of hFFA2-DREADD-HA mice responded to addition of MOMBA in single-cell Ca2+ imaging.
source: Single-cell Ca2+ imaging indicated that a proportion of these cells (37.2 ± 8.4% [mean ± SEM]) responded to addition of MOMBA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) whereas a markedly larger (p < 0.001) proportion (86.9 ± 6.5%, mean± SEM) responded to C3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: 86.9 ± 6.5% of cells from NDG of hFFA2-DREADD-HA mice responded to C3 in single-cell Ca2+ imaging.
source: Single-cell Ca2+ imaging indicated that a proportion of these cells (37.2 ± 8.4% [mean ± SEM]) responded to addition of MOMBA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) whereas a markedly larger (p < 0.001) proportion (86.9 ± 6.5%, mean± SEM) responded to C3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The effect of MOMBA on NDG cells was fully blocked by coaddition of CATPB.
source: The effect of MOMBA clearly reflected activation of hFFA2-DREADD-HA because, once more, this was fully blocked by coaddition of the hFFA2-specific antagonist CATPB (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In cells isolated from wild-type mice, no response to MOMBA was recorded (1.6 ± 1.0%).
source: Moreover, in equivalent cells isolated from wild-type mice no response to MOMBA was recorded (1.6 ± 1.0%, mean ± SEM) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), whilst a similar proportion of the cells (85.0 ± 5.5%, mean ± SEM) of the cells responded to C3.
evidence: This is demonstrated through calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: 85.0 ± 5.5% of cells from NDG of wild-type mice responded to C3 in single-cell Ca2+ imaging.
source: Moreover, in equivalent cells isolated from wild-type mice no response to MOMBA was recorded (1.6 ± 1.0%, mean ± SEM) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), whilst a similar proportion of the cells (85.0 ± 5.5%, mean ± SEM) of the cells responded to C3.
evidence: This is demonstrated through calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Functional hFFA2-DREADD-HA and FFA3 receptors are both present on cells of NDG.
source: These data indicate that functional hFFA2-DREADD-HA and FFA3 receptors are both present on cells of NDG but do not assess directly to what degree they may be coexpressed nor on which of the complex and diverse makeup of cells that comprise the NDG (Kupari et al., 2019) are these receptors expressed.
evidence: This is concluded from the calcium imaging data in NDG cells.

claim: Anti-HA immunostaining in DRG from hFFA2-DREADD-HA mice overlapped with PGP9.5 staining to a degree of 9.3 ± 5.8%.
source: As with NDG, whilst a degree of overlap of anti-HA immunostaining was observed with that for the neuronal marker PGP9.5 (9.3 ± 5.8%, mean ± SEM), which was both widely distributed and detected in tissue from both hFFA2-DREADD-HA-expressing (Figure 4A) and CRE-MINUS mice, the most intense anti-HA staining was in cells that were interspersed between the PGP9.5-positive neurons (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The most intense anti-HA staining in DRG was in cells that were interspersed between the PGP9.5-positive neurons.
source: As with NDG, whilst a degree of overlap of anti-HA immunostaining was observed with that for the neuronal marker PGP9.5 (9.3 ± 5.8%, mean ± SEM), which was both widely distributed and detected in tissue from both hFFA2-DREADD-HA-expressing (Figure 4A) and CRE-MINUS mice, the most intense anti-HA staining was in cells that were interspersed between the PGP9.5-positive neurons (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: X-gal staining corresponding to FFA2 promoter function was observed in DRGs from FFA2-KO-βGAL mice.
source: Consistent with HA staining, a similar pattern of expression was also observed with X-gal staining corresponding to FFA2 promoter function in tissue from FFA2-KO-βGAL mice (Figure 4B, left panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated through X-gal staining data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: X-gal staining corresponding to FFA3 promoter function was observed in DRGs from FFA3-KO-βGAL mice.
source: Furthermore, promoter function and hence expression of FFA3 (Figure 4B, middle panel) was also identified in DRGs by X-gal staining in tissue from FFA3-KO-βGAL mice.
evidence: This is demonstrated through X-gal staining data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: X-gal staining was absent in DRGs from wild-type littermates.
source: By contrast X-gal staining was absent in wild-type littermates (Figure 4B, right panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated through X-gal staining data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: 41.4 ± 10.0% of DRG cells from hFFA2-DREADD-HA mice responded to MOMBA in calcium imaging studies.
source: Addition of MOMBA produced a rapid and partially sustained increase in intracellular [Ca2+] (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D) in a substantial proportion (41.4 ± 10.0%, mean ± SEM) of the cells tested (Figure 4C and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: 82.1 ± 3.8% of DRG cells from hFFA2-DREADD-HA mice responded to C3 in calcium imaging studies.
source: By contrast addition of C3-promoted intracellular [Ca2+] elevation in most (82.1 ± 3.8%, mean ± SEM) cells (Figure 4D and Supplementary file 2) and this was generally more robust than effects of MOMBA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Initial stimulation by MOMBA did not prevent subsequent elevation of [Ca2+] in the same cells in response to C3 following washout of MOMBA.
source: Initial stimulation by MOMBA did not prevent subsequent elevation of [Ca2+] in the same cells in response to C3 following washout of MOMBA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through sequential calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: At least a proportion of DRG cells coexpress FFA2 and FFA3.
source: This indicates both that at least a proportion of these cells coexpress FFA2 and FFA3 and that exposure to MOMBA did not desensitize cells to subsequent exposure to C3.
evidence: This is inferred from the sequential stimulation experiments.

claim: Exposure to MOMBA did not desensitize DRG cells to subsequent exposure to C3.
source: This indicates both that at least a proportion of these cells coexpress FFA2 and FFA3 and that exposure to MOMBA did not desensitize cells to subsequent exposure to C3.
evidence: This is inferred from the sequential stimulation experiments.

claim: Responses to MOMBA were absent in cells derived from CRE-MINUS control mice.
source: Once more the effect of MOMBA was clearly an on-target effect of the ligand at hFFA2-DREADD-HA because responses to MOMBA were absent in cells derived from CRE-MINUS control mice and when cells isolated from hFFA2-DREADD-HA mice were preincubated with the hFFA2 receptor-specific antagonist CATPB (Figure 4C and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Responses to MOMBA were blocked when cells isolated from hFFA2-DREADD-HA mice were preincubated with CATPB.
source: Once more the effect of MOMBA was clearly an on-target effect of the ligand at hFFA2-DREADD-HA because responses to MOMBA were absent in cells derived from CRE-MINUS control mice and when cells isolated from hFFA2-DREADD-HA mice were preincubated with the hFFA2 receptor-specific antagonist CATPB (Figure 4C and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Effects of C3 on cells isolated from hFFA2-DREADD-HA mice were not blocked by CATPB.
source: By contrast, effects of C3 on cells isolated from hFFA2-DREADD-HA mice were not blocked by CATPB (Figure 4D and Supplementary file 2) and the proportion of cells that responded to C3 was not different in DRGs isolated from CRE-MINUS animals (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is demonstrated through calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The proportion of cells that responded to C3 was not different in DRGs isolated from CRE-MINUS animals.
source: By contrast, effects of C3 on cells isolated from hFFA2-DREADD-HA mice were not blocked by CATPB (Figure 4D and Supplementary file 2) and the proportion of cells that responded to C3 was not different in DRGs isolated from CRE-MINUS animals (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is demonstrated through calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: In DRG cells from hFFA2-DREADD-HA mice MOMBA stimulates Ca2+ mobilization via FFA2-DREADD-HA.
source: Together these data support the notion that in DRG cells isolated from hFFA2-DREADD-HA mice MOMBA stimulates Ca2+ mobilization via FFA2-DREADD-HA and C3 stimulates Ca2+ responses via FFA3.
evidence: This is concluded from the calcium imaging experiments with antagonists and knockout controls.

claim: In DRG cells from hFFA2-DREADD-HA mice C3 stimulates Ca2+ responses via FFA3.
source: Together these data support the notion that in DRG cells isolated from hFFA2-DREADD-HA mice MOMBA stimulates Ca2+ mobilization via FFA2-DREADD-HA and C3 stimulates Ca2+ responses via FFA3.
evidence: This is concluded from the calcium imaging experiments with antagonists and knockout controls.

claim: TUG-1907 produced substantial elevation of Ca2+ in isolated DRG-derived cells.
source: To further support the conclusion that responses to C3 in DRG-derived cells from hFFA2-DREADD-HA-expressing mice were indeed mediated via FFA3 we again employed the novel FFA3 activator TUG-1907 (Ulven et al., 2020). This ligand produced substantial elevation of Ca2+ in isolated DRG-derived cells (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is demonstrated through calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: TUG-1907 did not produce elevation of Ca2+ in DRG-derived cells isolated from FFA3 knockout mice.
source: As this ligand did not produce such effects in DRG-derived cells isolated from FFA3 knockout mice (Figure 4F), this confirmed the presence and functionality of FFA3 in hFFA2-DREADD-HA-expressing mice.
evidence: This is demonstrated through calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The ability of MOMBA to promote elevation of Ca2+ levels in DRG-derived cells was blocked by coincubation with FR900359.
source: The ability of MOMBA to promote elevation of Ca2+ levels in DRG-derived cells taken from hFFA2-DREADD-HA mice was blocked by coincubation with the Gαq/Gα11 inhibitor FR900359 (Schrage et al., 2015; Figure 4C and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through calcium imaging data with FR900359 shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Effects of MOMBA on DRG cells were unaffected by pretreatment with pertussis toxin.
source: By contrast effects of MOMBA were unaffected by pretreatment with pertussis toxin (Figure 4C and Supplementary file 1) which causes ADP-ribosylation of Gαi family subunits.
evidence: This is demonstrated through calcium imaging data with pertussis toxin shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Responses to C3 in DRG cells were blocked by pretreatment with pertussis toxin.
source: Very differently, responses to C3 were instead blocked by pretreatment with pertussis toxin, but not by treatment with FR900359 (Figure 4D and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated through calcium imaging data with pertussis toxin shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Responses to C3 in DRG cells were not blocked by treatment with FR900359.
source: Very differently, responses to C3 were instead blocked by pretreatment with pertussis toxin, but not by treatment with FR900359 (Figure 4D and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated through calcium imaging data with FR900359 shown in Figure 4D.

claim: FFA2 couples to Ca2+ signaling in DRG solely via Gq/11.
source: However, in DRG, we can conclude that FFA2 couples to Ca2+ signaling solely via Gq/11 because effects of MOMBA were fully attenuated when cells had been pretreated with the highly selective Gq/11 inhibitor FR900359 (Schrage et al., 2015).
evidence: This is concluded from the FR900359 inhibition experiments.

claim: Activation of each of FFA2 and FFA3 results in elevation of Ca2+ in DRG-derived cells, but the two receptors engage with different G proteins and use distinct mechanisms.
source: These results indicate that activation of each of FFA2 and FFA3 results in elevation of Ca2+ in DRG-derived cells, but that the two receptors engage with different G proteins and use distinct mechanisms to mediate these effects.
evidence: This is concluded from the differential effects of FR900359 and pertussis toxin.

claim: C3 produced a substantial increase in c-Fos-positive neurons in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord compared to saline in wild-type mice.
source: C3 produced a substantial increase in c-Fos-positive neurons compared to saline (p < 0.05) (Figure 5A, compare Figure 5B, C, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated through c-Fos immunostaining data shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: Introduction of MOMBA produced a significant increase in the number of c-Fos-positive neurons in the dorsal horn compared to saline in hFFA2-DREADD-HA-expressing mice.
source: Here, introduction of MOMBA also produced a significant increase (p < 0.05) in the number of c-Fos-positive neurons compared to saline (Figure 5A, compare Figure 5D, E, Supplementary file 3), although this was less extensive than produced by C3 in the wild-type animals.
evidence: This is demonstrated through c-Fos immunostaining data shown in Figure 5A, D, E.

claim: MOMBA did not promote an increase in c-Fos-positive neurons in the CRE-MINUS animals.
source: By contrast MOMBA did not promote such an effect in the CRE-MINUS animals (Figure 5A, compare Figure 5F, G), confirming this effect of MOMBA to reflect activation of the hFFA2-DREADD-HA receptor and that activation in the colon of both of FFA2 and likely FFA3 results in spinal activation.
evidence: This is demonstrated through c-Fos immunostaining data shown in Figure 5A, F, G.

claim: Activation in the colon of both FFA2 and likely FFA3 results in spinal activation.
source: By contrast MOMBA did not promote such an effect in the CRE-MINUS animals (Figure 5A, compare Figure 5F, G), confirming this effect of MOMBA to reflect activation of the hFFA2-DREADD-HA receptor and that activation in the colon of both of FFA2 and likely FFA3 results in spinal activation.
evidence: This is concluded from the c-Fos experiments in different mouse models.

claim: Perfusion of C3 into the colorectal region of hFFA2-DREADD-HA mice resulted in a significant increase in c-Fos-positive neurons.
source: To further confirm the contribution of FFA3, we perfused C3 into the colorectal region of hFFA2-DREADD-HA mice. This also resulted in a significant increase (p < 0.05) in c-Fos-positive neurons.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result.

claim: Preadministration of granisetron did not block spinal c-Fos expression in response to C3 or MOMBA in anesthetized hFFA2-DREADD-HA mice.
source: To assess whether 5-HT3 also plays a role in gut–spinal interaction induced by activation of SCFA receptors, the 5-HT3 receptor antagonist granisetron (1 µM) was administered prior to the administration of either MOMBA or C3. Preincubation with granisteron did not inhibit spinal c-Fos expression promoted by either MOMBA or C3 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, suggesting therefore, that the 5-HT3 receptor does not play a key role in this process).
evidence: This is demonstrated through c-Fos experiments with granisetron shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The 5-HT3 receptor does not play a key role in gut-spinal interaction induced by activation of SCFA receptors.
source: Preincubation with granisteron did not inhibit spinal c-Fos expression promoted by either MOMBA or C3 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, suggesting therefore, that the 5-HT3 receptor does not play a key role in this process).
evidence: This is concluded from the granisetron experiments.

claim: Gut sensory afferent neuronal firing is selectively enhanced by activation of FFA3 in the gut.
source: Firstly, we determine that gut sensory afferent neuronal firing is selectively enhanced by activation of FFA3 in the gut.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion based on the afferent nerve recording experiments.

claim: Gut-generated SCFAs can regulate spinal cord activity via both FFA2 and FFA3 receptors present in the gut, and at the level of extraspinal sensory ganglia.
source: Secondly, that functional FFA2 and FFA3 receptors, coupling via Gq and Gi G-protein subfamilies, respectively, are expressed by both neuronal and non-neuronal cells in DRG and NDGs and that gut-generated SCFAs can regulate spinal cord activity via both FFA2 and FFA3 receptors present in the gut, and at the level of extraspinal sensory ganglia (e.g., DRG/NDG).
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion based on multiple experimental findings.

claim: FFA2 couples via Gq G-protein subfamily in DRG and NDG.
source: Secondly, that functional FFA2 and FFA3 receptors, coupling via Gq and Gi G-protein subfamilies, respectively, are expressed by both neuronal and non-neuronal cells in DRG and NDGs and that gut-generated SCFAs can regulate spinal cord activity via both FFA2 and FFA3 receptors present in the gut, and at the level of extraspinal sensory ganglia (e.g., DRG/NDG).
evidence: This is concluded from the FR900359 inhibition experiments.

claim: FFA3 couples via Gi G-protein subfamily in DRG and NDG.
source: Secondly, that functional FFA2 and FFA3 receptors, coupling via Gq and Gi G-protein subfamilies, respectively, are expressed by both neuronal and non-neuronal cells in DRG and NDGs and that gut-generated SCFAs can regulate spinal cord activity via both FFA2 and FFA3 receptors present in the gut, and at the level of extraspinal sensory ganglia (e.g., DRG/NDG).
evidence: This is concluded from the pertussis toxin inhibition experiments.

claim: FFA2 and FFA3 are expressed by both neuronal and non-neuronal cells in DRG and NDGs.
source: Secondly, that functional FFA2 and FFA3 receptors, coupling via Gq and Gi G-protein subfamilies, respectively, are expressed by both neuronal and non-neuronal cells in DRG and NDGs and that gut-generated SCFAs can regulate spinal cord activity via both FFA2 and FFA3 receptors present in the gut, and at the level of extraspinal sensory ganglia (e.g., DRG/NDG).
evidence: This is concluded from the immunohistochemistry and calcium imaging experiments.

claim: SCFAs generated by gut microbiota-mediated fermentation of fiber can regulate central activity.
source: Perhaps most intriguing amongst the outcomes reported herein is the capacity for SCFA receptors that are activated by agonists introduced into the colon to cause activation of cells at the level of the dorsal horn of the spinal cord. These observations support a role for gut microbiota-derived SCFAs in directly co-ordinating and controlling responses between the gut and the central nervous system.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion based on the spinal cord activation experiments.

claim: The microbiota and their dysbiosis can be key contributors to a variety of long-term central nervous system deficits and malfunctions.
source: Given the rapidly emerging evidence that the microbiota and their dysbiosis can be key contributors to a variety of long-term central nervous system deficits and malfunctions (Ma et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2018; Cussotto et al., 2018; Rieder et al., 2017), the current studies provide insights into direct chemical links via a SCFA–gut–brain axis.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Pharmacologically targeting FFA2 or FFA3 might provide a therapeutic strategy for the treatment for various CNS disorders.
source: The fact that we can manipulate this axis via synthetic small molecule chemical ligands (e.g. MOMBA and TUG-1907) suggests that pharmacologically targeting FFA2 or FFA3 might provide a therapeutic strategy for the treatment for various CNS disorders (Silva et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings and supported by citation.

claim: FFA3 is known to selectively activate Gi G proteins.
source: This is also consistent with the effect of C3 being mediated by FFA3 in these cells, as FFA3 is known to selectively activate Gi G proteins (Brown et al., 2003; Stoddart et al., 2008a), and potentially proceeding via release of β/γ complexes from such Giα-containing G-protein heterotrimers (Smrcka and Fisher, 2019; Senarath et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: FFA2 can interact with and activate Gq-family G proteins as well as Gi-family members.
source: By contrast FFA2, and indeed the hFFA2-DREADD, in transfected cell lines is able to promote activation and downstream signaling via a wide range of G proteins including Gq/11 and Gi proteins (Hudson et al., 2012a; Bolognini et al., 2019; Brown et al., 2003; Stoddart et al., 2008a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: FFA2-mediated release of GLP-1 requires selective activation of Gq/11 family G proteins.
source: Whilst release of the hormone GLP-1 also requires selective activation of Gq/11 family G proteins (Bolognini et al., 2019), by contrast, our previous studies established that FFA2-mediated regulation of lipolysis is transduced by Gi-family G proteins (Bolognini et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: FFA2-mediated regulation of lipolysis is transduced by Gi-family G proteins.
source: Whilst release of the hormone GLP-1 also requires selective activation of Gq/11 family G proteins (Bolognini et al., 2019), by contrast, our previous studies established that FFA2-mediated regulation of lipolysis is transduced by Gi-family G proteins (Bolognini et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: In physiological cell types FFA2 appears to couple selectively to either Gi (adipose tissue) or Gq/11 (DRG and enteroendocrine cells).
source: Hence, in transfected cells although FFA2 shows the capacity to couple to each of Gq/11 and Gi and other G proteins (Bolognini et al., 2019), in physiological cell types the receptor appears to couple selectively to either Gi (adipose tissue) or Gq/11 (DRG and enteroendocrine cells).
evidence: This is concluded from the current and previous studies.

claim: Enteroendocrine cells can synapse with vagal neurons in mouse.
source: It has been established in mouse that enteroendocrine cells can synapse with vagal neurons (Kupari et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: PYY is expressed in similar subsets of enteroendocrine 'L-cells' as GLP-1.
source: Peptide YY (PYY) is expressed in similar subsets of enteroendocrine 'L-cells' as GLP-1 (Nohr et al., 2013; Lu et al., 2018) and perfusion of colonic tubes isolated from hFFA2-DREADD-HA mice with MOMBA also resulted in a rapid, markedly enhanced (p < 0.01), but in this case transient, release of PYY (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.
